newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to review troop presence in Africa - Millon.
newsitem.headline: France to review troop presence in Africa - Millon.

text.p: France said on Thursday that it planned to overhaul its military presence in Africa in line with reforms to turn its army into an all-professional force.
"It's obvious that there will be a review of our operations because the army will become totally professional," Defence Minister Charles Millon told Europe-1 radio.
"To maximise operational efficiency, we will reexamine the bases, our presence, the rotation of soldiers sent to Africa.
"We will study all that in full consultation with the African countries," said Millon, who added that France had 8,200 troops deployed on the continent.

He denied that the review was prompted by clashes in the Central African Republic. French troops launched an artillery and helicopter attack on army mutineers on Sunday, killing about 10 people, after two French officers were shot dead by rebels.
Asked whether the review would mean a cut in the number of French troops in Africa, Millon answered: "Our aim is to have exactly the same operational efficiency.
"So we will study the time French soldiers spend on African territory. Whether that is shortened, or whether we will send rotating missions is a technical problem, not a political one."
The move towards all-professional armed forces, part of a deep defence reform designed to modernise the military and increase its ability to operate overseas, was announced in 1995.
France's overall military strength will drop from half a million to 350,000 by the year 2002, with the number of troops serving abroad cut to 39,000 from 56,000.

Asked rules France had for intervening in African countries, Millon said: "France has cooperation and defence accords with a number of central African countries for political and historic reasons. France has a number of nationals in these countries and will ensure their protection."
In the Central African Republic, Millon said he hoped the country's democratic institutions would ensure a return to civil peace.
"(President Ange-Felix) Patasse was democratically elected. France has made a commitment and will respect it," he said.
